# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: Evolution, Lessons, and Next-Generation Platforms

The evolution of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has transitioned through several technological milestones: balloon angioplasty, bare-metal stents, and drug-eluting stents (DES) [1,2]. Despite the success of contemporary metallic DES in reducing restenosis, the permanent presence of a metallic cage inside the coronary artery carries long-term limitations. These include chronic local inflammatory responses, neoatherosclerosis, rigid restriction of natural vasomotion, and physical obstruction to potential future surgical revascularization [3,4]. To overcome these challenges, the concept of "vascular restoration therapy" emerged, introducing bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS). These devices were designed to provide transient mechanical support and antiproliferative drug delivery during the initial healing phase before undergoing complete resorption, thereby restoring the physiological integrity of the vessel wall [3,4].

The clinical journey of BVS began with the first-in-human evaluation of the PLLA-based Igaki-Tamai stent, demonstrating the feasibility of long-term scaffold resorption [5]. Subsequently, the first-generation polymeric everolimus-eluting Absorb BVS (Abbott Vascular) entered clinical trials. Initial evaluations in the ABSORB Cohort A [6] and B [7] trials demonstrated favorable vascular healing and scaffold resorption at 2 to 3 years. This led to several pivotal, large-scale randomized controlled trials, including ABSORB II [8], ABSORB III [9], ABSORB Japan [10], and ABSORB China [11]. Concurrently, investigator-initiated trials such as AIDA [12] evaluated BVS in real-world all-comer populations, while the blinded ABSORB IV trial [13] aimed to assess patient symptoms and clinical endpoints under more optimized conditions.

However, clinical experience with the first-generation Absorb BVS revealed a significant setback. Meta-analyses and pooled patient-level data at 1 year [14,15] and systematic reviews of scaffold thrombosis [16] revealed a significantly higher risk of target lesion failure (TLF) and scaffold thrombosis (ST) with BVS compared to cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents (EES). The final 5-year outcomes of the ABSORB III trial [17] and pooled 5-year individual patient-data meta-analyses [18] confirmed that the excess hazard of target vessel myocardial infarction and scaffold thrombosis persisted until complete resorption (around 3 years), after which event rates stabilized. The final 5-year results of the AIDA trial [19] and real-world registries like GHOST-EU [20] mirrored these safety signals. The primary mechanisms of BVS failure included thick struts (~150 μm) disrupting laminar flow, incomplete lesion preparation, underexpansion, malapposition, and late strut discontinuities or dismantling during the resorption process [21,22].

A major positive consequence of these setbacks was the recognition that BVS implantation technique is paramount. The "PSP" (Prepare the lesion, Size appropriately, Post-dilate with a non-compliant balloon) protocol was developed to ensure optimal scaffold expansion and apposition [23]. Clinical evaluations validated that strict adherence to the PSP technique significantly minimized the risk of both early and late scaffold thrombosis [24].

To address the mechanical limitations of first-generation polymeric scaffolds, next-generation bioresorbable platforms were developed, featuring thinner struts and alternative materials. Among these, magnesium-based resorbable scaffolds (MgBRS) offered higher radial strength and a faster resorption profile (~12 months). The BIOSOLVE-II trial demonstrated the feasibility and safety of the sirolimus-eluting Magmaris scaffold (DREAMS 2G) up to 12 months [25]. The large-scale, real-world BIOSOLVE-IV registry confirmed these results, showing low TLF rates and a highly favorable safety profile with a very low rate of scaffold thrombosis (<0.5%) under optimized implantation protocols [26].

In parallel, newer polymeric platforms with thinner struts emerged, such as the Fantom radiopaque tyrosine-polycarbonate-based scaffold (FANTOM II trial) [27] and the thin-strut PLLA-based MeRes100 scaffold (MeRes-1 trial) [28], both showing promising short- to mid-term outcomes. Furthermore, third-generation magnesium scaffolds, such as DREAMS 3G (Freesolve), with a further reduced strut thickness (99 μm), have demonstrated excellent 12-month safety, efficacy, and vasomotion restoration in the BIOMAG-I trial [29].

As highlighted by the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and European Association of Percutaneous Cardiovascular Interventions (EAPCI) task force, bioresorbable scaffolds remain a highly attractive concept for transient coronary scaffolding [30]. Today, the clinical application of bioresorbable technology is characterized by a refined approach: restricting use to highly selected patient and lesion cohorts, utilizing ultra-thin strut next-generation platforms, executing mandatory PSP protocols guided by intravascular imaging (IVUS/OCT), and prescribing tailored dual antiplatelet therapy to maximize patient safety and realize the true potential of vascular restoration.
